book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

chapters.relation: Reads the contrast between Jagger's shy private self and his stage persona as 'two Jaggers,' pointing to Gimme Shelter, where the strutting performer turns businesslike ('Whose war are we fighting, people?') and visibly stricken while reviewing the Meredith Hunter footage with Charlie Watts. The chapter recruits Nietzsche to explain the split: Jagger, the ex-LSE student who called the band 'my business,' has treated his own life as a work of art, becoming artist and artwork at once.

chapters.file: ch35 - A Little Help from Nietzsche.md
chapters.relation: Deploys Nietzsche's aesthetics—the Twilight of the Idols claim that the meaning of art is life itself, and the Birth of Tragedy line that existence is justified 'only as an aesthetic phenomenon'—to argue Jagger's self-invention is philosophy in action. It answers the puzzle of how one steps back from oneself to see an artwork: by creating the second, stage Jagger, the ordinary suburban guy imposes form on himself with Nietzsche's 'artists' cruelty' and becomes something crowds travel to watch.

Takes up the objection that living aesthetically is vanity (Carly Simon's 'one eye in the mirror') and answers with Jagger's 1969 Hyde Park eulogy for Brian Jones, where he read Shelley's Adonais—'Die, if thou wouldst be that which thou dost seek!' The chapter argues that self-ravishment creates glory energizing others, so a life made sublime in the Nietzsche-Shelley manner is wild exuberance rather than self-absorbed vanity.

chapters.file: ch37 - II - A Rolling Stone Gathers No Illusions.md
ch38 - Chapter 5 - The Head and the Groin of Rock.md
chapters.relation: Part 5 opener built on Keith Richards's quip that rock'n'roll 'starts from the neck down': Richards opposed playing Live Aid because 'nukes may obsess your brain, but they don't obsess your crotch.' The chapter stakes out rock as a felt, noncognitive, morality-free zone resisting co-optation by causes like No Nukes and Rock Against Racism, posing the head-versus-groin question the following sub-chapters test against Bentham and Mill.

chapters.file: ch39 - To Riff or Not to Riff.md
chapters.relation: Stages Bentham's hedonism through the riff-versus-soliloquy question: 'push-pin is of equal value with the arts and sciences of music and poetry,' pleasures differing only in quantity, so a Keith Richards riff that out-pleases Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' is simply the greater pleasure, and ranking pleasures 'higher' or 'lower' is prejudice. The chapter closes by noting Bentham's pleasure-pain calculus even expands the moral community to animals, setting up Mill's dissent on behalf of higher pleasures.

Takes Mill's side against the 'doctrine of the swine' slur on hedonism: music belongs to the higher pleasures produced by distinctively human faculties. The chapter then asks whether Darwinian continuity between humans and other primates undermines Mill's divide—whether the pleasures of rock'n'roll, which evolved primates developed alongside language and cave painting, rely more on our animal or uniquely human faculties, with 'Monkey Man' as the emblematic case.

Has the reader listen to 'It's Only Rock'n'Roll (But I Like It)' through headphones: the forty-four-second mark where a chorus and guitar part that sound like a horn section morph into a Chuck Berry riff shows that hearing is built from a lifetime of learned musical expectations. Quoting Mill's Autobiography on how music's pleasure 'fades with familiarity,' it argues the reverse happens too—a dynamic listener can be newly surprised by songs heard a zillion times.

Explains the Stones' pleasures neurochemically: a two-phase dopamine rush of anticipation and reward behind the spine-tingling moment of a song, the same pathway as life's four F's—feeding ('The Spider and the Fly'), fighting ('Street Fighting Man'), fleeing ('Before They Make Me Run'), and sex—and the one heroin exploits. Because there is no time to process every stimulus, prediction-making brains let mental models pass for reality, which is why frustrated and fulfilled musical expectations carry such a charge.

chapters.file: ch43 - Some Things Just Stick in Your Mind.md
chapters.relation: Shows how the twelve-bar I-IV-V blues schema works by delaying, frustrating, and finally satisfying learned expectations, citing Huron's Sweet Anticipation. From the performer's side, Keith's 'Guitar Workshop' study of Jimmy Reed—leaving notes out and droning open strings at maximum unresolved tension—explains the jacked-up chords of 'Jumpin' Jack Flash' and 'Gimme Shelter,' plus the fake-horn trick heard in 'It's Only Rock'n'Roll.'

Adjudicates the higher/lower dispute by disambiguating 'higher': a moral ranking Bentham rejects as prejudice, or a neurobiological-evolutionary distinction about distinctively human capacities that Mill can accept. Adopting Martha Nussbaum's reading of Mill in 'Mill between Aristotle and Bentham,' it concludes that rock'n'roll is both a lower pleasure (the same four-F dopamine pathways Keith insists on) and a higher one, imagining Mill teleported onto the tour bus for the demonstration.

chapters.file: ch45 - Chapter 6 - Paint the Flowers Black.md
chapters.relation: Part 6 opener: against the Beatles' 'Good Day Sunshine,' Jagger screams to see 'the sun blotted out from the sky,' and the chapter reads that darkness as rock's version of the post-Enlightenment attack (Nietzsche through Derrida) on philosophy's sunny rationalism, which Derrida names 'white mythology.' The Stones, 'the Nietzsche and Derrida of rock,' repudiate pop's optimism by returning to the blues of the oppressed and painting the white mythology of pop black.

Reads the Flowers album's blooms as dark—'Ruby Tuesday' can't be chained to a life where nothing's gained, and the heliotrope becomes Derrida's figure for philosophy forever turning toward its conceptual sun of truth, knowledge, or the good. That heliotropic bias, the metaphysics of presence, is illustrated by Augustine's treatment of evil as mere privation of good, which Nietzsche's genealogy of slave morality overturns by deriving good and evil from the same source, 'beyond good and evil.'

Chronicles Keith's mission from Life: turning 'white America's brains and ears around' to a blues tradition so marginalized that Muddy Waters did menial labor at Chess Records to stay on the payroll. Even the Stones' prettiest ballads—'As Tears Go By,' 'Have You Seen Your Mother Baby (Standing in the Shadow?)'—drag top-forty pop into the shadow, turning away the metaphysics of presence from inside the hit parade.

Traces the light-versus-darkness metaphor tradition from Plato's cave and Socrates' unexamined life through medieval 'illumination' and the Enlightenment to St. Paul's glass darkly, then lets Nietzsche ('shadow is as needful as light') and Derrida's deconstruction of presence/absence oppositions overturn it. The Stones do the same work in song: 'Just as every cop is a criminal, and all the sinners saints' in 'Sympathy for the Devil,' with 'Here Comes the Sun' overturned by 'Paint It Black' and 'Let It Be' by 'Let It Bleed.'

Uses 'Dandelion'—truth as a bright yellow flower that blows away—to mark the withering of Enlightenment confidence in plain, visible truth under deconstruction. Kierkegaard's 'truth is subjectivity' explains why truth on 'Get Off of My Cloud' cannot be shared directly ('Don't hang around 'cause two's a crowd'), and Nietzsche goes further: there is no truth to find, only wills to power making truths—'you can't always get what you want... you just might find you get what you need.'

Tells how the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper alter-egos provoked Their Satanic Majesties Request, a psychedelic misstep—'She's a Rainbow,' 'Dandelion'—that took the Stones away from their element after manager Andrew Oldham's departure. Beggars Banquet is the homecoming: 'Street Fighting Man' and Rev. Wilkins's 'Prodigal Son' return them, like prodigal sons, to their home in the blues 'with no expectation... to pass through here again.'

Pits Plato's Republic—censor the poets because they feed emotion against reason and offer only appearances, as a painter offers approximate representations—against Derrida and Nietzsche, who side with poetry: abstracting metaphors into concepts strips them of color, leaving a 'conceptual graveyard' of dead flowers, an 'abstraction without extraction.' The chapter's claim is that Plato prefers dead conceptual flowers while the Stones' 'Dead Flowers' and Nietzsche's forgotten metaphorical roots keep concepts alive.

Closes the part by pairing philosophy's bad boys with the band: Nietzsche and Derrida, misfits who reminded philosophy it is nourished by the metaphorical soil it disowned, have their analogue in the Stones, who reintegrated Black American blues into white rock'n'roll stripped of its African and slave origins. White music, like white mythology, had become an 'abstraction without extraction'—it needed to be painted black and to 'let it bleed.'

chapters.file: ch53 - Chapter 7 - Zen and the Art of Being a Stones Fan.md
chapters.relation: Part 7 opener, a fan's phenomenology: the author divides his life by Stones tours (the 1975 Tour of the Americas, the 1978 Some Girls tour), recalls his devout seventy-six-year-old father queueing six hours in Toronto for tickets 'because Keith is my favorite,' and describes the exponential pre-concert anticipation and the mystical magic of the opening notes. He closes by refusing the 'farewell tour' rumors and the media's age-ist clichés as celebrity trivialization.

chapters.file: ch54 - Hey Paparazzi, Get Off of My Cloud.md
chapters.relation: Coins 'celebrity profiling' on the model of racial profiling and runs through the stereotypes—'Indestructible Keith,' 'womanizer Mick,' 'homebody Charlie'—arguing no label can capture people who overflow them, even though Oldham's maxim 'there is no such thing as bad press' and the ashes-snorting anecdote show the Stones manipulate their image. Profiling also hid from a dismissing philosopher colleague that the Stones are essentially a live band that never plays 'Satisfaction' or 'Brown Sugar' the same way twice.

Recruits the 1941 comedy Ball of Fire, where Barbara Stanwyck teaches encyclopedia professors the conga by making them dance it instead of following floor diagrams: the Stones, like the conga, must be felt 'from the inside,' and celebrity profiling blocks that feel for their live performance. Admitting we will never know the objective truth about the past becomes a virtue, freeing the author's experimental return to ancient Greece.

Reconstructs the Greek world in which everything existing was aesthetikos—perception—with emotions like anger and erotic love moving as clouds that strike and possess us, and no transcendent God outside the kosmos. Its center is theoria: the collective ritual dancing of Dionysian festivals producing ekstasis, a god's-eye 'looking on' that later hardened into the theatron and finally Plato's abstract 'theory'—which is why a band inducing theoria at concerts counts as theorists in the original sense.

chapters.file: ch57 - Zen and the Art of Being a Stones Fan.md
chapters.relation: Draws the direct line from Dionysian festival to Stones concert: fans' intoxication, collective ritual dancing, and ecstatic 'looking on' at their own lives explain why the author organizes his biography around concerts. Songs like 'I can't get no satisfaction' and 'I'm shattered' shove systematically overlooked human realities in our faces, and a Prince Edward Island hostel's graffiti—'Zen is like the mind which understands The Rolling Stones'—completes the argument that the band shows the way to philosophy and a kind of religion.

Part 8 opener: distinguishes morality, immorality, and amorality, then argues that because people adopt moral codes they believe lead to happiness, hedonism—happiness through the fulfillment of desire and indulgence in pleasures—is a genuine moral code rather than immorality. Hence the reassurance that your wild nights of indulgent partying are actually your way of behaving morally, under a different code than your parents' or boss's.

Introduces Aristippus's Cyrenaics through Diogenes Laertius as the first systematic hedonists: all bodily pleasures good, better when more intense, frequent, and long-lasting, good 'even if it arises from the most unbecoming causes,' with happiness merely the sum of particular pleasures and pleasures of the flesh trumping pleasures of the mind. It maps this 'simple hedonism' onto 'Shake Your Hips,' 'Brown Sugar,' 'Rip This Joint,' and 'Out of Control,' with 'Monkey Man' as the movement's theme song.

chapters.file: ch60 - A Rolling Stone Gathers . . . Happiness.md
chapters.relation: Brings in Epicurus, speaking through Cicero, to correct the Cyrenaics: pursue pleasure rationally, declining pleasures that purchase greater later pains—Keith's drug-related legal bills, 'Sister Morphine's' desperation—and sometimes enduring pain for greater pleasure later, like kicking junk to enjoy raising children. Advocating simple living, a hierarchy of pleasures ranked by sober reasoning, and prudence (phronesis) as the chief virtue, it pictures modern Epicureans at a rock festival passing out condoms and running the needle exchange.

chapters.file: ch61 - What Can a Poor Boy Do.md
chapters.relation: Poses the part's question: Cyrenaic seize-each-fleeting-pleasure indulgence or Epicurean choosiness—which moral code is more likely to deliver happiness? First glance says the songs preach Cyrenaic hedonism, but a closer look finds the most hedonistic lyrics full of agonizing desire and unfulfilled pleasure rather than achieved happiness, hinting the Stones may not be recommending the Cyrenaic road at all.

chapters.file: ch62 - Now I Need You More than Ever.md
chapters.relation: Finds Epicurean confirmation in two songs: 'Let's Spend the Night Together,' where thwarted desire exacts bodily suffering ('tongue's getting tied... mouth's getting dry'), and 'Sister Morphine'—first written and recorded by Marianne Faithfull—where a dying addict is too weak to drag himself across the floor for the drug that is killing him. In both, pleasures bring pains so bad they can outweigh the goodness of the pleasure sought.

chapters.file: ch64 - Can You Always Get What You Want.md
chapters.relation: Considers the escape route that would save the Cyrenaics: perhaps the pain in the songs is merely the frustration of not attaining pleasure, not a cost of pleasure itself, in which case the Epicurean advice to prefer simple, easy pleasures stands. Weighing song-as-fiction against the documented hedonism of Jagger (seven children by four women) and Richards (five drug trials), it concludes such men do not lack access to pleasure, so the nagging unhappiness in the songs genuinely tells against Cyrenaic hedonism.

Delivers the verdict: Cyrenaic hedonism has been well tried by the Rolling Stones and clearly is not an effective road to happiness, so the Epicurean modification deserves its shot—keep the dedication to bodily pleasure but let prudence filter choices by their consequences. 'Waiting on a Friend' (choosing a friend over the game of 'making love and breaking hearts') and Exile's 'Happy' suggest the band already leans toward tempered hedonism and real satisfaction.

chapters.file: ch66 - III - Time Is on Rock’s Side.md
ch67 - Chapter 9 - From Main Street to Guyville.md
chapters.relation: Part 9 opener, narrative: fleeing Allen Klein and the taxman after the 1967 drug busts, the Stones settle at the mansion Nellecôte on the Riviera, recording Exile on Main St. in the basement with the Rolling Stones Mobile while Gram Parsons teaches Keith country classics. The album's title and its cover collage from Robert Frank's The Americans declare that these English exiles belonged, if anywhere, in America's freakish cultural circus.

Takes Liz Phair's claim that Exile in Guyville is a song-by-song response to Exile on Main Street seriously against the skeptical critical consensus—Jim DeRogatis, the anniversary liner notes, and her own doubting producer John Henderson, whom she silences with 'John! I did! Cross my heart and hope to die.' Since the claim never worked as marketing, the chapter proposes to figure out what it means, promising a philosophical explanation of the puzzlement rooted in assumptions going back to Plato's Academy.

Sorts the eighteen-to-eighteen song pairings into three relationship types: merely formal (tempo, key, structure), psychological or emotional (Phair treating Mick and Keith's songs like Rorschach inkblots and answering with her own associations), and critical or theoretical—a debate about exile, romance, and the human circus beyond songwriting craft. On a matched playlist you hear all three, from her clean Fender Duo-Sonic against Keith's crunchy Les Pauls to her vantage as a twenty-two-year-old woman launching a career in early-90s Chicago.

Introduces hermeneutics as something every reader already does: meaning is jointly created by the writer's intentions and a reader's own history and expectations, so the famous ambiguous 'yeeaaahhh' opening 'Rocks Off'—like Mona Lisa's smile—has no single fixed meaning. Artworks become fluid and multivalent (Their Satanic Majesties Request is alternately failure and underappreciated gem), artists interpret while creating, and meaning flows into metaphysics: 'More let it bleed than let it be.'

Asks how to know whether an interpretation of a lyric, a song, or a song-pair is trustworthy, and answers with coherence and Heidegger's hermeneutic circle: interpretation starts from a stockpile of assumptions and must circle back to revise them as new evidence enters, until, in Martin Eger's phrase, it converges rather than oscillating forever between opposing poles.

chapters.file: ch72 - Really You Guys Are into Music.md
chapters.relation: Defines Guyville as Chicago's predominantly male indie-rock scene in Bucktown and Wicker Park (Urge Overkill, Smashing Pumpkins, Material Issue), which Phair confronted head-on: 'Really? Okay, so you guys are into music. Watch—I can make music.' But beyond being a woman's take on a male musical world, the chapter announces her real subject—what exile really means on Main Street, distinguishing romantic, geographical, and existential exile from one's self.

chapters.file: ch73 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Pairs the tenth tracks in the romantic-exile register: Keith's 'Happy' ('I need a love to keep me happy,' with Anita and Marlon in tow) against Phair's 'Fuck and Run,' where she wakes alarmed among men who get out of bed citing 'a lot of work to do'—wishing for exactly the bond Keith has. In 'Loving Cup' versus 'Mesmerizing' the roles flip: where Mick begs for 'a little drink from our loving cup,' Phair wants to be the mesmerist casting the spell.

chapters.file: ch74 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy.md
ch75 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Pairs 'Sweet Black Angel'—Mick and Keith's freedom song for Angela Davis, the philosophy professor imprisoned in 1970 on murder charges and called 'a sweet black slave'—with Phair's eerie piano piece 'Canary,' which puts herself in a cage 'like a good canary' who learns her name, works up to her potential, earns her meat, and comes when called. Phair transforms Davis's prison chains into the chains of a proper Winnetka girl's education, ending with contemplated domestic terrorism: 'Send it up on fire, death before dawn.'

chapters.file: ch76 - Mick and Liz Partners in Crime.md
chapters.relation: Argues Phair is not just responding song-by-song but cast herself as the women of Main Street: her 'Never Said' keeps a rendezvous with Mick's 'Tumbling Dice' philanderer secret, 'Flower' answers 'Let It Loose' with a lover's 'perfect suck-me size' lips, and 'Glory' answers 'Shake Your Hips' with a 'really big tongue'—hardly accidental given the Jagger lips-and-tongue logo Jim Pasche designed in 1971. Her opener '6’1”' diagnoses the man who can 'only get my rocks off while I'm sleeping' as one who has 'long since passed understanding what it takes to be satisfied,' a vine with no resting point.

chapters.file: ch77 - With You It’s Always Take, Take, Take.md
chapters.relation: Confronts Phair's NPR account—that she wrote '6’1”' about a crush on Urge Overkill's Nash Kato, superimposing Mick's Exile character on him and writing as the girl 'Rocks Off' brushes past—yet treats it as another interpretive layer rather than a refutation, since she called Jagger's performance 'a perfect portrait' of Kato. Using Martin Eger's 'cascade of interpretations,' it shows Mick interpreting his own life, Phair interpreting Mick through Kato, and the author interpreting Phair: 'It's interpretations... all down the line.'

Answers the anti-relativist who holds Main Street's greatness self-explanatory: if its meaning has nothing to do with what Liz Phair thinks, it has nothing to do with what the fundamentalist thinks either. The skeptics' error—expecting Guyville to sound like Main Street—inherits the Platonic-Aristotelian assumption that inspiration means imitation (knowing a statue's beauty means containing a copy of its shape), whereas the Stones themselves 'responded' to Muddy Waters and Chuck Berry without merely imitating; Phair's closer 'Strange Loop,' its riff morphing into '6’1”,' closes the hermeneutic circle and invites us to revisit, not finalize, Exile.

holes.name: Life as a Work of Art (giving style to one's character)
holes.what: Nietzsche's idea (Twilight of the Idols, The Gay Science) that one should survey one's strengths and weaknesses and fix them 'into an artistic plan,' so that existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon.
holes.why: Chapters 34-36's entire reading of Jagger's two personas—artist and artwork at once—rests on this Nietzschean self-stylization, which no existing slug covers.

holes.name: White Mythology
holes.what: Derrida's notion that Western philosophy's abstract reason is a disguised metaphorics that whitens and universalizes its own European origins while effacing, marginalizing, and denying what it excludes.
holes.why: Chapter 45's thesis—that the Stones repudiated sunny pop's 'white mythology' by painting it black and returning to the blues—names and applies this concept throughout.

holes.name: The Metaphysics of Presence
holes.what: The Western privileging of what is present (being, light, the good) over what is absent, forgetting the conditions by which the present comes to be—Derrida's name for philosophy's heliotropic bias.
holes.why: Chapters 46-48 apply this doctrine explicitly, reading the Stones' shadows, darkness, and 'Paint It Black' as deconstruction of pop's privilege of light and presence.

holes.name: Theoria (festival seeing and ekstasis)
holes.what: The ancient Greek practice of collective ritual seeing at Dionysian festivals—music and dancing that produced ekstasis, 'standing outside oneself' with a god's-eye look on the world—from which 'theatre' and abstract 'theory' both descend.
holes.why: Chapter 56's whole argument that Stones concerts are modern Dionysian theoria, making the band 'theorists' in the original Greek sense, is built directly on this unlisted concept.

holes.name: Aristippus of Cyrene
holes.what: Founder of the Cyrenaics, the first systematic hedonists, who held immediate bodily pleasure—however unbecoming its cause—to be the good, with happiness merely a sum of particular pleasures.
holes.why: Chapter 59 reads 'Brown Sugar,' 'Out of Control,' and 'Monkey Man' as expressions of Aristippus's Cyrenaic 'simple hedonism,' which the following chapters contrast with Epicurean hedonism.

holes.name: The Hermeneutic Circle
holes.what: Heidegger's principle that interpretation always begins from a stockpile of prior assumptions and must circle back to revise them, with good interpretations converging on coherent understanding.
holes.why: Chapter 71 makes the hermeneutic circle (with Martin Eger's convergence test) the yardstick for whether readings of Guyville's song-by-song responses to Exile are trustworthy.

holes.name: Imitation Theory of Art (mimesis)
holes.what: The Platonic-Aristotelian view that art works by imitation—artworks copy appearances, and knowing something means the mind containing a copy of its shape or harmonies.
holes.why: Chapter 78 argues critics dismissed Liz Phair's 'song-by-song response' because this inherited assumption equates inspiration with imitation, which her hermeneutic account of Guyville overturns.
